final.memo:
AIG operates a collection of international insurance and retirement businesses that, under normal circumstances, would be the type of franchise we admire [D01]. However, the core business is fundamentally obscured by a financial-products subsidiary that has entered into opaque derivative contracts [D01]. This structure makes it impossible to define the company's future, as the derivative exposure creates potential liabilities that are not bounded by reported figures [D01].

We require businesses with predictable economics and consistent returns on capital, yet AIG reported a $13.16 billion net loss for the first six months of 2008 [D01]. The firm is currently under extreme capital stress, and its reliance on massive collateral to back its derivative portfolios introduces an existential risk to the entire enterprise [D01].

In our view, the management team is currently struggling to navigate an environment where liquidity needs remain unknown and potentially catastrophic [D01]. While they have initiated reviews to protect capital, the company's survival is not a given [D01]. We never bet on survival in a situation where the risks are this opaque.

The market is currently pricing AIG as a potential failure because of these derivative exposures [D01], [D05]. We cannot see a reason to classify this as a bargain when the floor for the business is essentially non-existent [D01]. It is better to hold cash for safer, more predictable opportunities than to risk our capital—and our reputation—on a binary outcome of this magnitude [D01].
